evidence.source: 說文解字（online transcription of 大徐本, with 段玉裁注）
evidence.field: 牀 entry; component analysis and definition
evidence.text: The entry gives 牀, ‘安身之坐者’ (‘a seat/resting place for the body’), and analyzes it as 从木、爿聲: 木 is the semantic element and 爿 the phonetic. 徐鍇 offers a different historical explanation, treating 爿 as a shortened form of a reclining-person shape; 段玉裁 rejects the claim that the compound should be reanalyzed as 牀省聲 and discusses 爿 as a distinct element. The source’s record is the traditional graph 牀, not 床.
evidence.title: 說文解字「牀」 - 說文解字在線查詢

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 床/牀 variant relationship; cited dictionary forms
evidence.text: The entry treats 牀 as the traditional/base graph and 床 as its popular form, citing 玉篇: ‘床，俗牀字’. It quotes 干祿字書 as classifying 床 as vulgar, another form as common, and 牀 as standard; it also quotes 廣韻 defining 牀 and noting 床 as vulgar. The modern standardization adopted 床 as the standard graph. This supports 床 as a variant-form relation to 牀, not a claim that 床 is an earlier ancestor.
evidence.title: 牀 (床) - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 爿 entry; ancient form and semantic account
evidence.text: This source analyzes oracle-bone 爿 as a vertically written bed shape and calls 爿 the initial graph for 牀, with bed as its original meaning. It says the graph later came to be used mainly as a component, and that 木 was added as a semantic marker in 牀 because beds were often wooden. It cites oracle-bone use as a place name in 合集 36969 (‘在爿’), and treats the bed reading as supported in part by the bed-like element in 疒. This is the source’s paleographic account; the database page gives no date for the cited oracle-bone inscription in the displayed entry.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 爿

evidence.field: 牀 entry; graphic attestations and readings
evidence.text: The page lists examples under 金文, 楚系簡帛, 說文小篆, 秦系簡牘, and 隸書. Its named examples include a late Warring States bronze, 包山 2.260, Qin Shuihudi 日甲125, and Eastern Han slips/stone inscriptions. It gives modern Mandarin chuáng, Cantonese cong4, Tang transcription *jrhiɑng, and Middle Chinese 崇母 陽韻 平聲 with fanqie 士莊切. The listed inscription sequence documents the graph; it does not by itself establish a chronological sequence of senses.
evidence.title: 牀 chuáng - 漢典

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart, Old Chinese reconstruction database
evidence.text: For 牀, the table gives Mandarin chuáng, Middle Chinese dzrjang, and Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *k.dzraŋ, glossed ‘bed’. This is a reconstruction for the word written 牀, not an independent reconstruction of the sound of an original depicted object. It supports a broad phonological comparison for the graph’s reading but does not supply a separate pronunciation for 爿 in its proposed graphic role.
evidence.title: Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1 (by radical and stroke count)

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 床 definition and cited early textual glosses
evidence.text: The entry cites 說文 defining 牀 as a place for sitting/resting, 玉篇 as a couch/seat for resting, and 廣韻 as ‘簀’ while quoting the 易 phrase ‘遜于牀下’. It also cites 淮南子 and later literary examples for furniture, supports, flat surfaces, and the classifier use. These establish multiple documented senses and examples but do not give a full dated pathway linking all senses. The dictionary associates 易 and 說文 with early senses; it does not date the composition or earliest surviving witness for each quoted text.
evidence.title: 床 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: 漢字ペディア, Japan Kanji Aptitude Testing Foundation
evidence.text: The entry lists Japanese on-readings ショウ・ソウ and kun-readings ねだい, こしかけ, ゆか, とこ, だい. Its meanings include bed, seat, floor, and platform, and it explicitly identifies 牀 as the original graph of 床. This is evidence for Japanese readings and senses, not evidence that the character or word originated in Japan.
evidence.title: 牀 | 漢字一字 | 漢字ペディア

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 床 entry; Shuowen analysis and variant history
evidence.text: The entry says 床 is written 牀 in Shuowen, analyzed as 木 plus phonetic 爿. It cites 玉篇 calling 床 a popular form of 牀, and reports that the popular form later became the standard graph. This supports a nonchronological variant relation for 床 versus 牀 and identifies 广 as part of the later written form; it does not support treating 广 as the historical phonetic component.
evidence.title: 床 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 爿 entry; ancient form, semantic account, and oracle-bone citation
evidence.text: The database interprets oracle-bone 爿 as a vertically written bed and calls 爿 the initial graph for 牀, with bed as its original meaning. It says 木 was added as a semantic element in 牀, and cites an oracle-bone place-name use in 合集 36969, ‘在爿’. That citation establishes an early graph use, but the entry does not date the individual inscription or prove that the cited use means bed.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 爿

evidence.field: 牀 entry; definition and component analysis
evidence.text: The online Shuowen transcription gives 牀, ‘a place for resting the body’, and analyzes it as 从木爿聲: 木 is the semantic element and 爿 the phonetic. This is Shuowen’s historical analysis, not independent proof of the components’ original object or an exact sound match.
evidence.title: 說文解字在線查詢: 第367頁

evidence.field: 牀 entry; readings, senses, graphic attestations, and Shuowen note
evidence.text: The entry records Mandarin chuáng; Middle Chinese 崇母 陽韻 平聲, 士莊切; Tang transcription *jrhiɑng; and lists graphic examples from late Warring States bronze, Chu bamboo/slips, Shuowen small seal, Qin Shuihudi slips, and Han clerical writing. It also records senses including a sitting/lying piece of furniture, a rack, a well enclosure, a bed-shaped implement, a base, and classifier uses. These listed attestations and glosses do not by themselves establish a complete dated semantic pathway. Its transcription of Xu Shen gives 木 as semantic and 爿 as phonetic, while later commentators disputed the reconstruction of 爿 as a shortened reclining-person shape.
evidence.title: 牀 chuáng - 漢典

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart, Old Chinese reconstruction database
evidence.field: 牀 pronunciation; Middle and Old Chinese reconstructions
evidence.text: For the word written 牀 ‘bed’, the database lists Mandarin chuáng, Middle Chinese dzrjang, and Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *k.dzraŋ. This supplies a historical reconstruction for the word written 牀, not an independent reconstruction of the object depicted in 爿. The inspected entry does not supply 爿 as a separate phonetic reconstruction.
evidence.title: Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1 (by radical and stroke count)

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 床 entry; dated-source quotations and senses
evidence.text: The entry quotes Shuowen, Y upian and Huainanzi for sitting/resting furniture; cites Southern Dynasties and Northern Zhou examples for racks and furniture supports; and gives later examples for bed-like surfaces and classifier use. It records several senses and cited works but does not date the composition or earliest surviving witness of each text, or establish when one sense extended into another.
evidence.title: 床 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.field: File description; Warring States bronze-style glyph candidate and license
evidence.text: The file page describes a digital vector depicting 牀 in a Warring States bronze-script style and lists Sinica Database, Chinese Etymology, CUHK Multi-function Chinese Character Database, Chinese Text Project, and Chinese Linguipedia among available sources. The page dedicates the file under CC0 1.0. This is a modern digital redraw, not a photograph or facsimile of an ancient artifact.
evidence.title: File:牀-bronze-warring.svg - Wikimedia Commons

evidence.field: File description; Qin slip-style glyph candidate and license
evidence.text: The file page describes a digital vector depicting 牀 in Qin slip script and associates it with the Sinica database example 71.E5FE, annotated 睡. The page states public-domain dedication under CC0 1.0. It is a modern redraw based on a script example, not an image of the excavated slip.
evidence.title: File:牀-slip.svg - Wikimedia Commons

evidence.field: File description; oracle-bone-style 爿 glyph candidate and license
evidence.text: The file page identifies a digital vector as an oracle-bone-style 爿 glyph and cites a Sinica database image, 42.F033, with note 菁11.18 合21574. It gives CC0 1.0 reuse terms. This is a modern redraw, not a photograph of an oracle bone; use as a candidate for the graph-form tradition, while the source identification of 爿 as a bed remains an interpretive account.
evidence.title: File:爿-oracle.svg - Wikimedia Commons

evidence.field: Old Chinese pronunciation of 床/牀
evidence.text: The opened entry lists the Zhengzhang (2003) Old Chinese reconstruction for the bed word written 床 as *zraŋ. It separately lists Mandarin chuáng and Middle Chinese dzrjang; these are different periods and transcription systems.
evidence.title: 床 - 维基词典，自由的多语言词典

evidence.text: In its Zhengzhang (2003) phonetic-series table, the entry lists 爿 with *zaŋ, alongside *braːn as an additional reconstruction. The source therefore does not give only *zraŋ for 爿. The table lists 床/牀 as *zraŋ. This supports a same-system comparison of the entries, but not a claim that 爿’s independently reconstructed pronunciation was *zraŋ.
evidence.title: 爿 - 维基词典，自由的多语言词典

evidence.field: 牀 phonetic-series analysis and pronunciation comparison
evidence.text: The opened entry labels 爿 as the phonetic component and 木 as semantic in 牀. Its table of characters in the 爿 phonetic series attributes Zhengzhang (2003) forms *zaŋ (also *braːn) to 爿 and *zraŋ to 牀. This is secondary presentation of the reconstruction and component analysis, not direct confirmation from Zhengzhang’s published source.
evidence.title: 牀 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

gaps: The dossier’s competing claims that 床 is an ideographic compound or that 广 is phonetic are not supported by the inspected authoritative accounts: the inspected historical dictionaries instead explain 床 as a popular graphic variant of 牀, whose stated analysis is 木 semantic + 爿 phonetic. No separate direct paleographic inspection of the glyph images was performed.

The CUHK database reports oracle-bone 爿 as a bed and cites an oracle-bone place-name use, but the page excerpt does not date those attestations or show the specific glyph image in this research record. The earliest securely dated attestation of the bed word and the exact chronology of 爿 versus 牀 remain unestablished here.

The retrieved evidence supports 爿 as a sound component in the Shuowen account of 牀, but did not provide a reliable, independently checked historical reconstruction for 爿 itself within the same reconstruction system. The proposed sound role is attributed to Shuowen; its phonological comparison cannot be independently evaluated from these sources alone.

The historical semantics are not a chronology: ‘seat/resting place’, bed/couch, platform/support, floor-like surface, and classifier uses are documented in different sources and periods, but this research did not establish when or through which specific semantic links each extension arose.

No external evidence was found that establishes a loan origin for the word 床/牀 from Khmer, Mon, Burmese, or Vietic. The cross-language comparisons mentioned in the dossier remain unverified here; neither the bed graph’s phonetic analysis nor the reconstruction of the Chinese word alone proves such borrowing.
The source packet’s Japanese definition and readings are consistent with reference entries, but the inspected evidence does not establish a Japanese-origin graph or Japanese semantic chronology.

CUHK’s oracle-bone interpretation of 爿 as a bed is a paleographic source assertion; the cited 合集 36969 use is glossed as a place name, and the inspected page did not date the inscription. The earliest securely dated use of the bed word and the chronology between the simple 爿 graph and compound 牀 are not established here.

Shuowen identifies 爿 as phonetic in 牀, and the available comparisons include modern Mandarin chuáng and the Baxter–Sagart reconstruction of 牀 *k.dzraŋ. The inspected Baxter–Sagart table did not provide an independently checked reconstruction for 爿 in the same system, so the sound fit cannot be independently assessed here. The reconstructed word pronunciation does not establish the name or pronunciation of the depicted object.

No inspected evidence established the dossier’s proposed Khmer, Mon, Burmese, or Vietic borrowing relationship. Those comparisons cannot be confirmed from the character’s phonetic analysis or reconstruction alone.

Dictionaries record furniture, rack/support, well enclosure, bed-shaped object, base, and classifier uses in citations from multiple periods, but the sources inspected do not document dates for each earliest textual witness or establish a full semantic chain. Gloss order is not treated as chronology.

The Warring States bronze, Qin slip, and oracle-bone candidates are digital redrawings. The Commons pages provide named database leads and reuse terms, but these research findings do not claim visual inspection of candidate pixels or independent verification against the original artifacts.

The inspected pages attribute the reconstructions to Zhengzhang (2003), but are secondary sources; this search did not verify the pair against Zhengzhang’s original publication or a direct authoritative reconstruction database.

The same-system values are not identical as listed: 爿 has *zaŋ (and an additional *braːn), while 床/牀 has *zraŋ. The phonetic-series relationship is reported by the source, but these entries alone do not establish the sound history or exact phonetic fit.

No new primary paleographic evidence was inspected in this focused source check. The dossier’s cited account that 爿 served as a phonetic element in 牀 remains a historical source assertion; uncertainty about the early depicted referent or name of 爿 is separate from this pronunciation comparison.
